1948年，皮耶爾·莫尼雄在法國創製和聲手風琴，1952年取得專利。原型由喬瓦尼: In 1948 Pierre Monichon created the harmoneon in France and took out a patent in 1952. The prototype was built by Giovanni Segalla in Paris, and it was later made by makers such as Portolo Busato and entered the catalogues of several accordion firms. Its keyboard does away with preset chords and uses the same fingering on both hands, and it was intended for playing with orchestras. In 1949 Monique Lecoq-Taupin gave the first performance, of Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro; in 1956 she formed the first duo with Charles Taupin. In 1968 a course was set up at the Paris Conservatoire, and from 1974 it was taught in conservatoires; it is played mainly in France, the Netherlands and Germany, and interest has revived in recent years.

The reeds inside are of brass or stainless steel, which keeps the tone stable and lasting. The keys and buttons are of ivory or plastic, and the hand straps and shoulder straps of leather or synthetic material. Its range is wide, covering everything from the full resonance of the low register to the clear tone of the top, with rich and varied shades of timbre. The instrument sounds through the vibration of free reeds, and its resonance is distinctive and deep, which gives it carrying power. Beside the traditional accordion the harmoneon sounds finer and gentler; beside the button accordion its tone is softer and more delicate. Beside wind instruments it keeps the singing, continuous quality of the accordion family while offering richer changes of timbre and more room for expression, and it suits both classical and modern works.

The harmoneon is a French free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.132, created by Pierre Monichon in 1948. It is built like the duet concertina and the button accordion, with a keyboard system using the same fingering on both hands and no preset chords, which makes the left hand lighter and the tone of the two sides more even. The instrument was designed for concert use and can play with a symphony orchestra; it was later played in France, the Netherlands and Germany and entered conservatoire courses.
